Task Four: Control Flow Practice
Now is the opportunity to utilize conditional logic; before diving in, let’s define a new character column for each data frame

We’ll create a for loop while using if/else logic to classify the type of blood pressure measurements after receiving the treatment in the first group:

for (i in 1:20){
  if (updated_bp_data_1$post_bp_1[i] <= 120){
    updated_bp_data_1$status[i] = 'optimal'
  } else if ((updated_bp_data_1$post_bp_1[i] > 120) & (updated_bp_data_1$post_bp_1[i] <= 130)){
    updated_bp_data_1$status[i] = 'borderline'
  } else if (updated_bp_data_1$post_bp_1[i] > 130){
    updated_bp_data_1$status[i] = 'high'
  }
}

Task 1: Conceptual Questions

If your working directory is myfolder/homework/, what relative path would you specify to get the file located at myfolder/MyData.csv?

You need to back out of the “homework” folder because the file you want is just in “myfolder”, so you would use the relative path “../MyData.csv”

What are the major benefits of using R projects?

The major benefit to using R projects is that it tells your code where to find files without needed to specify full path names, since R will look for the file being called within the folder that the project is in. This makes it easier to share your work. R projects also have their own workspace and history.

What is Git and what is GitHub?

Git is a version control software. To use it, it needs to be installed on your computer. GitHub is a website that stores files. Git can work between GitHub and your local computer to pull files from GitHub and then push your changes back to GitHub. GitHub is helpful for working with teams, but everyone needs to have Git on their computers.

What are the two main differences between a tibble and a data.frame?

A tibble is a fancy type of data frame that has extra structure to make it easy to understand what you’re looking at when you print it. The basic structure is the same as a data frame, but it prints out nicely, showing you the dimensions and automatically only shows a small subset of the rows (no need to use the head() function and tells you how many more rows there are.
Another difference is that using tidyverse functions on a tibble will produce a tibble rather than simplifying down, if the output could be simplified down.

Task 1: Conceptual Questions

If your working directory is myfolder/homework/, what relative path would you specify to get the file located at myfolder/MyData.csv?

In order to access the previous folder in the working directory, the relative path you would specify to get the file would be “../MyData.csv”. The notation “..” tells R to move up one folder or directory from “homework” into “myfolder”.

What are the major benefits of using R projects?

The major benefit to using R projects is that it tells your code where to find files without needed to specify full path names, since R will look for the file being called within the folder that the project is in. This makes it easier to share your work. R projects also have their own workspace and history.

What is Git and what is GitHub?

Git is a version control software that tracks changes made to files and allows us to view those very changes. It also manages branching and merging too. Github is the online platform that hosts Git repos and makes it easy to store, share, and even collaborate with others on projects.

What are the two main differences between a tibble and a data.frame?

A data.frame is a straight-forward collection of vectors of the same length, but can have different types. Names can easily be assigned to these vectors and certain elements can be accessed via [ , ] or $. A tibble has a lot of similarities to a data.frame except the display of a tibble only shows a handful of rows and provides more details about the variables in the data set; it’s also easier to rename things with a tibble.
Whenever an error occurs, a tibble will notify you unlike a data.frame, and tibbles also have more strict notations that doesn’t allow partial column name matching.

Interquartile Range
Write a function that takes a vector of numbers and returns the interquartile range:

getIQR <- function(inputVector) {
  if(!is.vector(inputVector) | !is.numeric(inputVector)){
    stop('Input must be a numeric vector.')
  }
  # Subtract the 25th percentile from the 75th percentile
  unname(quantile(inputVector)[4] - quantile(inputVector)[2])
}

What is meant by long format data and wide format data? Which do we generally prefer for statistical analysis?

Long format data refers to multiple rows for each observational unit (e.g. recurring ID numbers for test scores such as math/reading)–this is generally the preferred format for statistical analysis because it is expected by many R functions from visualization libraries (ggplot2) to statistical modeling functions (lm/ANOVA/mixed effects models).
Wide format data generally has one row for each observational unit with different measurements separated by columns (e.g. one ID number followed by a math column and a reading column).
